boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Hatteras Inlet Batteries record (August 28-29, 1861) in Blockade of the Carolina Coast [August 1861]. The August 26 departure from Hampton Roads, the later occupation of the inlet and the Confederate reinforcement attempts from the sound are context. Campaign-wide movements, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. Imported numerical estimates remain unchanged; this pass does not validate them as simultaneous opening forces.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads '9th and 20th New York regiments (est. 2,000) [US]; Hatteras Island Garrison (900) [CS]'; the live field reads 2,000 (US 2,000; CS 0). Stringham says the transports carried parts of two regiments and a company of regulars. Martin says he had about 350 men at the post when the fleet appeared, that the forts needed at least 225 to work the guns, and that reinforcements of 60, 73, 64 and 50 men with their officers reached him on the evening of the 28th. NPS gives the garrison surrendered on the 29th as 670, and the compilers note that Stringham's omitted prisoner list contained 670 names.
claims.rationale: The frozen US figure is marked an estimate; the frozen 900 and the surrendered 670 are different populations from Martin's garrison at the start. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live Confederate zero is not measured absence.

Stringham says the fort's colors came down early on the 29th, which many took for surrender, but no attention was paid because the same had happened the day before, before the fort fired on the Monticello.
claims.rationale: Observations from the two reports; no signal log inspected.

claims.value: The frozen and live commanders are Major General Benjamin Butler and Colonel William F. Martin. NPS says Butler and Stringham led the expedition. Stringham commanded the squadron's attack, Butler took passage on the flagship and went into the inlet in the tug Fanny to take possession, and the articles of capitulation were signed by Stringham and Butler and by Barron, Martin and Andrews. Martin says he and Major Andrews gave command of the defenses to Commodore Barron on the evening of the 28th, before the surrender.
claims.rationale: Command roles from the two reports and a summary. The listed Confederate commander had handed over command before the capitulation; Butler's own reports are in Army Official Records Volume IV, which was not inspected. No automatic sole credit.

claims.value: The frozen and live results read Union victory. Stringham reports the flags down on both forts at 12:25 p.m. on the 28th, Fort Clark occupied, and a white flag at 11:10 a.m. on the 29th, followed by unconditional capitulation; Martin says Fort Clark was abandoned when its ammunition ran out and the garrison fell back to Fort Hatteras.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 773 (US 3; CS 770); the live field reads 673 (US 3; CS 670). NPS says the Federals lost only one man. Stringham says there was no accident to a single officer or man of the Navy, Army or marines and that he could not get a correct list of the enemy's killed and wounded; his prisoner list is described by the compilers as 670 names. Martin reports one and possibly two men killed on the 28th and doubts the accuracy of his captains' returns.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Prisoners taken at the capitulation are counted in the frozen and live Confederate totals; they are not a separate battle loss.

open_questions: Butler's reports and the other Army reports (Army Official Records Series I, Volume IV, pp.579-594, per the Navy compilers' footnote) were not fetched: that volume is being registered in another pass. Barron's and Andrews's reports, Gillis's and Stellwagen's reports and the Confederate telegrams were read but not selected under the three-family ceiling; Martin's enclosed returns are not printed.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Stringham's August 30, September 2 and September 3, 1861 reports (Navy Official Records Series I, Volume 6) are one family of interested Union naval accounts; the articles of capitulation printed with the August 30 report were signed jointly by both sides. William F. Martin's August 31, 1861 report (same volume, copied by the compilers from a newspaper clipping) is one family of interested Confederate accounts. The Navy volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. No Scribner history narrates the engagement; Nicolay mentions the Hatteras victory in one clause.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
